title: Ricky Hatton suffering from degenerative brain disease at time of death, inquest told
content:
Ricky Hatton was suffering from a degenerative brain disease that may have affected his behaviour and meant he did not intentionally take his own life, an inquest heard.

A pathologist’s examination revealed that the former world champion boxer, aged 46, was suffering from chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), almost certainly a legacy of his long career in the ring.

“As a boxer, Mr Hatton would have sustained repeated blows over his career,” the pathologist, Neil Papworth, explained in his report.

Although CTE can lead to behavioural changes, memory loss and mood swings, Papworth went on to state that it was “not possible to determine precisely” whether the abnormalities in Hatton’s brain contributed to the events leading to his death.

Hatton was discovered at his house, known as Heartbreak Hotel, in Hyde, near Manchester, by his manager, Paul Speak, on September 14 last year. He had hanged himself with a bedsheet, but the coroner, Alison Mutch, said she could not give a verdict of suicide and cited the presence of CTE among her reasons.

“I cannot be satisfied that he intended to take his own life,” Mutch said, as Hatton’s family members wept in court. “Intent remains unclear as he was under the influence of alcohol and a neurological post-mortem found evidence of CTE.”

The inquest at South Manchester coroners’ court was told that Hatton had been found in the games room of his house. The lights were on, with the television playing music, and there was an empty bottle of wine on the pool table, plus a half-filled glass on the side. The police found no note and that was also cited in the coroner’s findings.

Toxicology reports found Hatton had been drinking shortly before his death and, for context, would have been more than two and a half times the legal drink-drive limit. Other tests showed previous cocaine and cannabis use, but nothing to indicate that he had been taking drugs in the hours before his death.

Hatton, nicknamed ‘The Hitman’, established himself as one of Britain’s most popular boxers during a 15-year career in which he won 45 of his 48 professional bouts.

At his peak, he was a two-weight world champion, winning titles in the light-welterweight and welterweight divisions. He also fought Floyd Mayweather in 2007 and Manny Pacquiao, but lost both fights.

However, his life as an elite sportsman was accompanied by personal issues that, at one point, saw him admitted to the Priory clinic, the inquest was told.

“Post-boxing, my dad had mental health issues and also issues with alcohol and cocaine,” his son, Campbell, said in a statement to the inquest. “He openly spoke about these as a mental health ambassador.”

Campbell, a former boxer himself, went on to say that his father had seemed to be in “the best place for years” but had significant issues of memory loss, repeated himself constantly and completely forgot conversations so often that he needed to write stuff down to remember.

His father, he explained, could be “confused and forgetful” after a boxing career in which he “lived his life in and out of the ring at 1110 per cent”.

Hatton had made a number of plans for the future and, on the day he was found, he was due to be flying to Dubai to take part in an exhibition boxing match. This, Campbell said, “leads us to believe it (Hatton’s death) wasn’t pre-meditated”.

Other evidence presented to the inquest also made it clear that Hatton was “making positive plans” and thinking about the future, including going to an Oasis concert, taking his daughters, Fearne and Millie, to Tenerife and arranging other holidays.

His mother, Carol, recalled the last time she had seen him alive, asking him why he had been tempted to box again. “You could be hurt,” she told him.

“No,” her son replied. “Don’t worry, I’ll sort it.”

He had been more concerned, she recalled, about Campbell, who had some issues of his own after leaving boxing. “I’m not bothered about his boxing career,” Hatton told her. “I just want to help my son.”

Carol went on to say they had also talked about him planning to sell his house and downsize to a smaller place. He was often at home alone, he told his mother, and mentioned that no one ever used the swimming pool. Then, saying goodbye, his mother told him she loved him. His final words to her were: “Love you too, Mum.”

“The last hug he gave me almost broke my ribs,” said Carol.

On the day before he was found, Hatton had been out with his daughters, aged 12 and 13, and seven-year-old grand-daughter for a meal. Nothing was out of the ordinary, the inquest heard.

In some of the more emotive evidence, his former partner, Jennifer Dooley, described the couple’s daughters as being “heartbroken” and talked about how they used his pillows to sleep at night, wore his old T-shirts and sprayed his aftershave.

They had gone to Tenerife with him last summer and, according to Jennifer, he loved taking an active part in their lives, whether it be attending school events or joining in with their TikTok videos.

“He was very much the fun dad and the girls loved that about him,” said Jennifer. “Both girls described that summer as the best one ever with their dad. The girls were especially excited about the prospect of seeing their dad box.”
